name: Vardic Holds
summary: A loose confederation of northern Holds that turned an old seafaring culture into an industrial one without giving up its values: craft, reputation, oaths, and leaving behind something worth remembering.
government: A confederation of Holds, each under its own Jarl and its own laws, bound by the Compact of Nine Anchors and deliberately weak at the centre.
knownFor: Heavy industry, shipyards and ironclads, maker's marks and named machines, keeping your word, and testing things first.
gateAttitude: The unknown is something to master: they tend to see the Gates as another frontier to enter, understand and master.
beliefs:
Most Vards follow the **Old Gods of the Holds**, less a church than a way of seeing the world through **Fate, Making and Memory**. Creation isn't finished, and gods and mortals both keep shaping it, which is why a well-made ship or engine is, in a small way, an act of faith. Everything leaves a thread in the **Great Weave**; fate is the tension of all those threads pulling on each other, and what you control is the kind of thread you leave. A promise is a thread. So is a betrayal, and so is a ship and the name painted on it.

The worst death is the **final death**: being completely forgotten. At a funeral the reciter lists what the dead person did, the mourners stand one by one to add what she missed, and she closes with *"Now he is ours to remember."* The tradition cares more *that* the dead are remembered than *where* they go.

Five gods are known everywhere: **Veyr**, the First Smith, of fire, craft and invention; **Ragna** of the Far Shore, of voyages and those who don't come back, now the patron most Vardic Expeditioners name first; **Haldor** the Oathkeeper, of promises and vengeance on oathbreakers; **Skara** Under the Mountain, of death, ancestry and memory (grave, not evil); and **the Wanderer Without a Name**, of strangers, luck and world-changing accidents. In the **Forging of the Sun**, Veyr forged the sun from something beneath the world, couldn't hold it, and cast it into the sky: *"Then let it burn where no roof can contain it."* Engineers quote it when an experiment surprises them. **Ragna** sailed so far the stars changed; the ship came home and she didn't, and since the Gates some Vards wonder whether that story was more literal than anyone thought. The **Nameless King** demanded to be remembered and had his name taken away; a few enthusiasts claim the unattributed Valeoran Ruins are his monuments, which scholars treat as folklore-driven speculation.

Day to day, serious oaths are sworn before Haldor aloud with witnesses, and Expeditioners say Ragna's name before a crossing and mark their gear so something carries their thread home. A minority in the ports follows the **Faith of the First Light**, with no northern communion of its own.
history:
The northern homeland is fjords, islands, mountains and cold sea, where travel by water is easier than over the next ridge. Kings have united large parts of it more than once, and their kingdoms rarely outlived a few generations. What lasted was the **Hold**: a settlement, its land and the people attached to its **Jarl**, who might inherit the seat, be elected or follow some custom of that Hold. A Vard's first loyalty is still usually to a Hold, and that's a choice the Vards keep making, not a failure of unity.

In the **Age of Oars** foreign chronicles remember the raiding; the Vards remember that prestige came from going somewhere unfamiliar and coming back with something worth singing about. That link between **exploration and reputation** is a big part of why so many Vards took to the Gates.

Coal and metallurgy brought the **Furnace Century**: forges became foundries and shipyards, shipwright dynasties became engineering houses, and the maker's marks and knotwork moved from longships onto engines and ironclads. The **Hrafneld**, built by **Sigrun Veyrsdottir**, was the first industrial ship that looked unmistakably Vardic, with a long low hull and an iron raven at the prow. At its launch a foreign observer called it *"a barbarian longboat wrapped in iron"*, and she answered without looking away from the ship: *"Then perhaps you should avoid meeting it at sea."*

Foreign powers used the rivalries that wealth sharpened, and the **Wars of Smoke** burned factories and wiped out some older Holds. They ended when nine jarls met on ships anchored in neutral water at **Skeld Sound**, because none trusted the others enough to meet on land. The **Compact of Nine Anchors** says: no foreign power may seize recognised Vardic territory, each Hold keeps its own laws, and every Hold helps when the north faces a common threat. When an Aurelian envoy offered Jarl Stenvar a free deep-water harbour, the jarl asked only whether the Empire's flag would fly over it, and on hearing *"Naturally"*, told him to build it somewhere else.

**The Gates.** The Vardic instinct is practical: *if something can't yet be forged, tested or understood, the problem is temporary.* Direct experiment is far more acceptable here than in Verna or Tianzhao. The Gates are also a place where a shipwright's apprentice can come home with a name. The best-known story: while the University proposed a long analysis of an apparently indestructible fragment from the Green Vault, the metallurgist **Edda Skorn** put it on her anvil and hit it with a hammer. The hammer broke. She said *"Excellent."* What the joint Vardic–Vernan research on it found hasn't been made public.
visualSummary:
You can usually tell something is Vardic before you see the mark on it: heavy, practical, built for cold and wet, and never anonymous. The motifs are **knotwork, wings, anchors and diamonds**, and the raven still turns up on prows and clasps. Ornament is welcome on something that already works, and never allowed to make it harder to repair. Ports sit where the mountains meet the water: long steep-roofed timber halls beside foundries, iron cranes and drydocks, with standing stones older than any of it at the harbour mouth.

Almost everything carries a **maker's mark**, which is closer to a signature on a promise than a brand: if the hull fails, everyone who looks at the wreck knows whose fault it was. Important machines get **proper names** (a pumping engine called *Grim Old Halla* is expected to run for forty years), and the highest honour a maker can receive is **Veyrsson** or **Veyrsdottir**, "child of the Smith", given and never claimed. People can earn an epithet the same way, like *Kari Brenn, Who Kept the Crane*.

Clothing is heavy wool, reinforced leather, fur at the collar and personalised metal fittings, with Hold colours and knotwork marking rank; Hold guards still wear the old mail on ceremony, while soldiers in the field carry rifles. The usual stereotype is the loud barbarian fond of axes, which Vards find more tiresome than offensive; the culture that built the Hrafneld is precise and deeply technical. They judge a stranger by three questions: what have you done, does your work hold up, and do you keep your word?

relations.text: Old naval rivalry and mutual respect.
Admiration for engineering; impatience with political argument.
Strong trade ties, distrust of debt.
Mutual respect for craft; disagreement over metaphysical caution.
Mutually useful, methodically at odds: Verna wants to study it first, the Vards want to test it.

extraRule: Once per session, when you Create an Advantage using **Crafts** by repairing, reinforcing, modifying or improvising equipment, you may treat a tie as a success with one free invoke instead.
